title: Ultraviolet light-induced fluorescence in chiropterophilous flowers: a potential complementary signal for bat pollination
content:
Abstract
Chiropterophily is a specialized pollination syndrome shaped by reciprocal adaptations between nectar-feeding bats and flowering plants. Although bat pollination of flowers is traditionally considered to depend mainly on olfactory and acoustic signals, growing evidence suggests that visual signals, including ultraviolet (UV) sensitivity in bats, might also contribute to floral detection. We evaluated UV-induced floral fluorescence in chiropterophilous species from arid environments of the Baja California Peninsula and compared it with bird- and insect-pollinated species. Flowers were photographed under white light and UV illumination at 365 and 395 nm. Fluorescence intensity was quantified using a relative fluorescence index, calculated as the ratio between flower and background luminance. Generalized linear models assessed the effects of wavelength, pollination syndrome, species identity, and their interactions on fluorescence responses. All species exhibited detectable fluorescence, although intensity varied among taxa and illumination conditions. UV light at 365 nm produced the strongest fluorescence contrast, particularly in chiropterophilous species, such as Pachycereus pringlei, Stenocereus thurberi, and Agave sobria. Wavelength, pollination syndrome, species identity, and the interaction between wavelength and pollination syndrome significantly affected relative fluorescence index values. These findings support the hypothesis that floral fluorescence might function as a complementary visual signal for nectar-feeding bats.
